claims.text: The as-cast Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti baseline is superconducting.
The as-cast Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti alloy has a high defect density.
The as-cast Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti alloy has substantial random atomic disorder.
Annealing at progressively higher temperatures between 600 and 1000 °C will progressively increase short-range atomic order.
A suitable annealing window can increase atomic order without causing phase separation.
Increasing short-range atomic order reduces defect-induced electron scattering.
Reducing disorder and defect scattering increases the electron mean free path.
Compositional and structural disorder in this alloy acts as pair-breaking scattering centers.
The superconductivity of the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti system is consistent with conventional BCS-type phonon-mediated pairing.
The highly disordered superconducting phase can be described in the dirty-superconductor limit.
Increasing the mean free path by annealing strengthens electron–phonon coupling in the dirty limit.
Modest annealing-induced ordering will lower residual electrical resistivity relative to the as-cast state.
Modest annealing-induced ordering will sharpen the superconducting transition relative to the as-cast state.
Modest annealing-induced ordering may slightly increase Tc relative to the as-cast state.
The as-cast baseline has a broader superconducting transition than a modestly ordered annealed state.
Strong defect-induced scattering lowers Tc in the as-cast baseline.
Excessive annealing can produce phase separation or unintended intermetallic phases.
Secondary-phase formation can degrade or complicate the superconducting response.

contradictions.description: Secondary-phase formation is defined as outside the hypothesis's valid domain in the boundary field, but superconducting changes associated with secondary phases are also presented as refuting the hypothesis. An out-of-domain result cannot cleanly serve as a decisive falsification without a predeclared phase-pure subset or exclusion rule.
